page: Amazon Web Services m7i.metal-24xl is a bare-metal general-purpose server powered by dedicated 4th Generation Intel Xeon 8488C processors. Built on the x86_64 architecture, the system provides 48 physical cores and 96 vCPUs running at a base frequency of 3.2 GHz, supplemented by 105 MB of L3 cache. It delivers 384.0 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. Hardware-level acceleration flags include Intel AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions), AVX-512 with VNNI, and cryptographic enhancements such as AES and SHA-NI. The platform features a baseline network throughput of 38 Gbps, lacks bundled local storage, and contains zero GPUs.

Benchmark measurements indicate exceptional computational throughput across highly parallel execution paths. The instance achieves top-tier results in multi-core metrics, including a Geekbench multi-core score of 21,748.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 88,761.09. Clang software compilation and ray tracing tests also position the system in the top 10% bracket. Single-core performance remains reliable with a Geekbench single-core score of 2,176.0 and a stress-ng single-core rating of 2,069.3. Memory bandwidth reaches 231.55 GB/sec for large uncached block reads, pairing well with network throughput to support high-volume operations like Redis SET commands at 106.61 million operations per second.

Given its bare-metal architecture and high physical core density, the server provides significant resource efficiency for heavy compute and enterprise server virtualization, eliminating hypervisor overhead. The presence of AMX instructions enables viable CPU-based machine learning inference, demonstrated by processing speeds of 292.47 tokens per second on 7B models. However, the total absence of bundled local storage requires external network-attached volumes for persistent data, which should be factored into overall architecture design.

The m7i.metal-24xl is well-suited for high-density container orchestration, enterprise relational databases, large-scale CI/CD build pipelines, in-memory caching layers, and CPU-driven matrix workloads that demand direct hardware access and extensive multi-threading capability.
